statement: In adults followed in prospective cohort studies of drinking and death (published 1981 to 2021, mostly from North America, Europe and Australia), drinking a little (about 1.3 to 25 g of ethanol a day, from one 10-g drink a week to about two drinks a day) compared with not drinking: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of dying from any cause, and the question is disputed. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them, who in most studies included people who had stopped drinking or drank occasionally, people who drank a little died at lower rates: in a 2006 pooled analysis of 34 cohorts (1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths) the death rate was lowest at 6 g a day, about half a drink (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), and stayed lower up to 42 g a day; in 87 and then 107 cohorts (up to 4,838,825 people and 425,564 deaths) the relative risk at 1.3 to 25 g a day was 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90, and 0.83 to 0.88). These analyses give relative risks only, so the difference cannot be given as a number out of 100 (editors' observation). The difference shrinks or disappears as the comparison group is defined more strictly: people who had stopped drinking, some of them because of illness, died at higher rates than abstainers in the main models (relative risks 1.22 to 1.38); against occasional drinkers, people who drank a little had no lower death rate (1.02, 0.95 to 1.10; 0.97, 0.85 to 1.11 after adjustment), while abstainers had a higher one with limited adjustment (1.19, 1.12 to 1.27) but not after adjustment (1.04, 0.94 to 1.16); after adjustment for study characteristics, including how each study defined its non-drinkers, the estimate was 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) in 87 cohorts and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) in 107; in the 13 cohorts that compared with people who had never drunk it was 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06); and in the 6 cohorts that did so and had recruited people at a median age of 55 or younger, 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), against 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89) in 18 older cohorts whose non-drinkers included former and occasional drinkers. Even in 2006, cohorts whose comparison group left out former and light drinkers showed a smaller reduction (16% against 23% at the lowest point) that ended at 30 rather than 52 g a day. The 2016, 2023 and 2024 analyses are by one research group and reuse the same cohorts; the 6-cohort estimate rests on studies the article does not name and allows anything from a 13% lower to an 11% higher death rate (editors' arithmetic); and genetic studies, which avoid the non-drinker comparison, concern heart disease and diabetes rather than deaths from all causes (see the answers on the heart). None of these designs can show whether drinking a little itself makes people live longer or shorter. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: In many large studies, people who drank a little (up to about two 10-gram drinks a day) died at slightly lower rates than people who did not drink. But in most of these studies the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some because they were ill, and people who drank now and then. When people who drank a little were compared with occasional drinkers, or with people who had never drunk, there was no clear difference, though the few studies that made the strictest comparison cannot rule out a small gain or a small loss. These studies cannot show whether a little alcohol itself helps, harms or makes no difference to how long people live, and researchers disagree.
population: Adults in prospective cohort studies of drinking and death from any cause published from 1981 to 2021, pooled in a 2006 meta-analysis (34 cohorts to December 2005) and in three analyses by one research group (87 cohorts to 2014; 107 to July 2021; subgroups of the 107); mostly from North America, Europe and Australia, with some from Asia; drinking reported at the start of each study
exposure: Drinking a little, as reported at the start of each study: about 1.3 to 25 g of ethanol a day in the 2016, 2023 and 2024 analyses (low volume: from one 10-g drink a week to about two drinks a day), and intake in grams a day on a continuous scale in the 2006 analysis (lowest death rate at 5 to 8 g a day)
comparator: Non-drinkers as each study defined them (in most studies including former and/or occasional drinkers); in subgroups, lifetime abstainers (people who never drank) or occasional drinkers (under 1.3 g a day); in the 2006 analysis, each study's lowest-intake category
outcome: Death from any cause, as relative risks (no death rates by drinking group are reported)
magnitude: Di Castelnuovo et al. 2006 (34 cohorts, 56 curves, 1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths; fixed-effect; against each study's lowest-intake category): lowest relative risk 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83) at 6 g a day, lower mortality significant up to 42 g a day; adjusted at least for age 17% lower (99% CI 15% to 18%) at 6 g, up to 37 g; with light or former drinkers in the reference group 23% (20% to 26%) at 8 g, up to 52 g; without them 16% (14% to 18%) at 5 g, up to 30 g; the same 34 curves 19% (17% to 21%) crude and 16% (14% to 18%) adjusted. Stockwell et al. 2016 (87 cohorts, 3,998,626 people, 367,103 deaths), low volume 1.30 to 24.9 g a day: against study-defined abstainers 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90), occasional 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), former 1.22 (1.14 to 1.31); against occasional drinkers, low volume 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10), abstainers 1.19 (1.12 to 1.27); with all study-level covariates, low volume 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07), former 1.38 (1.24 to 1.54); six covariates 0.89 (0.84 to 0.94); 13 lifetime-abstainer studies 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), former 1.31 (1.09 to 1.57); 7 higher-quality studies 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15) without one influential study. Zhao et al. 2023 (107 cohorts, 4,838,825 people, 425,564 deaths): unadjusted low volume 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88); fully adjusted 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01; P = .07), occasional 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06), former 1.26 (1.12 to 1.42); against occasional drinkers, fully adjusted, low volume 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11), abstainers 1.04 (0.94 to 1.16); I2 above 85.87% in every category. Stockwell et al. 2024 (subgroups of the 107; random study effect): all 107, 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88; 99 studies with low-volume estimates); 6 studies of cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger against lifetime abstainers 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without the random effect; with a 30-day intake measure as well, 5 studies, 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15); older cohorts with both abstainer biases, 18 studies, 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89); one criterion only, 0.88 (0.84 to 0.92; 51 studies) and 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95; 18 studies); editors' calculation of the difference between 0.98 and 0.84, treating the two sets of studies as independent: ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), p of about .03. No absolute death rates by drinking group in any of the four.

risk_of_bias.note: The comparison groups of most cohorts include former and/or occasional drinkers; drinking was self-reported, mostly once; each cohort adjusted for different confounders; the 2016 and 2023 adjusted estimates are study-level (ecological) models calculated at unstated covariate values; all four reviews are rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_di_castelnuovo_2006, sc_stockwell_2016, sc_zhao_2023, sc_stockwell_2024).

inconsistency.note: Estimates run from 0.81 to 1.04 depending on the comparison group and study features, which the abstainer biases partly explain; within categories heterogeneity remains large (I2 61% to 84% in 2016, above 85.87% in 2023; in 2006 the deviance fell from 879.4 to 154.0 with random effects).

indirectness.note: Death from any cause is measured directly; cohorts are mostly from high-income countries and middle-aged at entry, which the claim states.

imprecision.note: The estimates against study-defined non-drinkers are precise, but those least exposed to the biases are not: 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11) from 6 cohorts, 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06) from 13, and 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) after adjustment, each compatible with a meaningful reduction and with no difference or an increase.

publication_bias.note: Egger tests found no evidence in 2016 and 2023; not assessed in 2006 or for the 2024 subgroups.

dose_response.note: The lower rate is a dip at low intake, not a gradient.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding and former drinkers in the comparison groups would more plausibly create than hide a lower death rate; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on whether drinking a little changes the risk of dying: the lower death rate against study-defined non-drinkers is consistent, but whether it reflects alcohol or the make-up of the comparison groups is disputed, and the estimates least exposed to the biases are too imprecise to show either a benefit or its absence. Overlapping evidence: Stockwell et al. (2016), Zhao et al. (2023) and Stockwell et al. (2024) are one group's analyses of largely the same cohorts (the 87 are among the 107, and the 2024 subgroups are drawn from the 107), and Di Castelnuovo et al. (2006) shares many cohorts with them, so their agreement on the unadjusted pattern is counted once, not as independent replication. Genetic (Mendelian randomization) studies are observational too: using gene variants linked to drinking addresses some confounding, but effects of the variants through other routes (pleiotropy), weak instruments, selection (for example analyses split by drinking status) and the inability of most to show a curve at low intake remain; here they are cited only second-hand, through the review the GBD 2020 authors cite, and for heart disease and diabetes, not deaths, so they do not change this rating and are rated in the answers on the heart. The editorial (Chikritzhs et al., 2015) frames the debate and is not counted as evidence. Status contested: credible evidence and critiques point both ways (METHODS §6.4, §7).

debate.question: Do people who drink a little live longer because of the alcohol, or is the lower death rate seen in many studies explained by who the non-drinkers are?
debate.evidence_yes: Pooled cohort studies consistently find lower death rates in people who drink a little than in non-drinkers as the studies defined them. In 34 cohorts with over a million people (Di Castelnuovo et al., 2006; sc_di_castelnuovo_2006; funded by the Italian research ministry, no financial disclosures reported), the pooled curve was lowest at 6 g a day (relative risk 0.81, 0.80 to 0.83); the reduction held in curves adjusted at least for age (17%) and for social status and diet as well (18%), and in cohorts whose comparison group left out former and light drinkers (16% at 5 g a day); within the same studies, adjustment moved the lowest point only from 19% to 16% lower, from which the authors argue that unmeasured confounding as strong as the measured kind would still leave more than 10%. In 87 and 107 cohorts the pooled relative risk at 1.3 to 25 g a day was 0.86 (Stockwell et al., 2016, sc_stockwell_2016; Stockwell et al., 2024, sc_stockwell_2024), and after adjustment for study characteristics the point estimates stayed below 1 (0.97, 0.88 to 1.07, in 2016; 0.93, 0.85 to 1.01, P = .07, in Zhao et al., 2023, sc_zhao_2023), as did the estimate in 13 cohorts that compared with people who had never drunk (0.90, 0.76 to 1.06). A pooled analysis of individual data from 83 cohorts reproduced the U-shaped curve for deaths from any cause when never and former drinkers were included (Wood et al., 2018; sc_wood_2018; values in an appendix not read). The lower rate fits observational findings for the heart: in the Global Burden of Disease review of 592 studies, ischaemic heart disease was the one condition whose risk was significantly lower at low intake (lowest relative risk 0.86 in men at 0.83 standard drinks of 10 g a day and 0.82 in women at 0.92; Griswold et al., 2018; sc_griswold_2018); the heart findings, observational and genetic, are rated in the answers on the heart.
debate.evidence_no: How much lower the death rate looks depends on who is in the comparison group, as the abstainer-bias argument predicts. Of 87 cohorts, 65 counted people who had stopped drinking among their non-drinkers and 50 counted occasional drinkers; only 13 compared with people who had never drunk (Stockwell et al., 2016; funded by the US National Institutes of Health; no statement of the authors' interests). People who had stopped drinking died at higher rates than abstainers in the main models (relative risks 1.22 to 1.38), and the 2006 authors note that former drinkers may have stopped because of health problems. Against occasional drinkers instead of abstainers, people who drank a little had no lower death rate (1.02, 0.95 to 1.10; 0.97, 0.85 to 1.11 after adjustment). Adjusting for study characteristics moved the estimate from 0.86 to 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) in 87 cohorts, and from 0.85 to 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) in 107 (Zhao et al., 2023; partly funded by the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction through a Health Canada grant for Canada's guidance on alcohol and health). In the 6 cohorts that recruited people at a median age of 55 or younger and compared them with people who had never drunk, the relative risk was 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), or 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without allowing for differences between studies, against 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89) in 18 older cohorts whose non-drinkers included former and occasional drinkers (Stockwell et al., 2024; partly funded by the same centre under a contract for that guidance; three authors declare earlier funding from government alcohol monopolies, and two travel support from an organization that advocates against alcohol use). Even in 2006, cohorts whose comparison group left out former and light drinkers showed a smaller reduction that ended at a lower intake (30 against 52 g a day). Genetic studies avoid the non-drinker comparison: by a review that the Global Burden of Disease 2020 authors cite, 67% of such studies of heart and blood-vessel disease and 75% of those of diabetes found no association with alcohol (Bryazka et al., 2022; sc_bryazka_2022). A 2015 editorial by six alcohol researchers, three of whom wrote the 2016 review, argued on these grounds that the case for protection was so undermined that the field was due for repositioning, and that guidelines and burden estimates should assume no protection (Chikritzhs et al., 2015; sc_chikritzhs_2015; no interests declared).
debate.neither_can_show: Whether alcohol itself makes any difference: every study is observational, drinking was mostly reported once at the start, and people who never drink differ from people who drink in more than drinking (in the one analysis that compared them, in sex, ethnicity, smoking and diabetes; Wood et al., 2018), so even the strictest comparison cannot separate alcohol from the reasons people do not drink; cohorts recruited younger also contribute deaths at other ages and from other causes (editors' observation). The adjusted estimates of 2016 and 2023 come from models of study characteristics, not of people, calculated at covariate values the papers do not state. The decisive 6-cohort subgroup is not named in the article, its participants and deaths are not counted, no measure of disagreement between its studies is given, and its difference from the older cohorts is not tested in the article (editors' calculation from the printed intervals: ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.34, p of about .03). The four analyses share most of their cohorts (the 87 cohorts of 2016 are among the 107 of 2023 and 2024, all by one group), so their agreement is not independent, and all four rate critically low on a standard checklist for reviews (AMSTAR 2: for example single-database or English-only searches and no list of excluded studies). The genetic studies concern heart disease and diabetes, not deaths from all causes, and only five of 24 tested a curved relation that could show an effect at low intake. No source read gives death rates out of 100 or 1,000 for people who drink a little and people who do not.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the cohort studies read, people who drink a little die at somewhat lower rates than non-drinkers as most studies define them (relative risks of about 0.81 to 0.86, that is 14% to 19% lower), and that pattern is consistent across many cohorts. But it is largest where the non-drinkers include people who stopped drinking or drink occasionally, and it shrinks to no clear difference where the comparison is with occasional drinkers or with people who never drank, above all in cohorts recruited younger; those estimates are few and imprecise, so neither a small benefit nor a small harm can be ruled out. The editors therefore do not read these studies as showing that drinking a little makes people live longer, nor as showing that it shortens life: the designs read cannot tell. Both sides' main estimates agree that people who had stopped drinking, and people drinking 45 g a day or more (1.12 to 1.44 in the 2016 analysis), died at higher rates than abstainers (see the answer on the amount at which drinking starts to shorten life).
debate.what_would_settle_it: A pooled analysis of individual data from cohorts that record drinking from early adulthood and repeatedly, with people who never drank and stable occasional drinkers as separate comparison groups and former drinkers counted at the amounts they used to drink, reporting death rates out of 1,000 under an adjustment set fixed in advance; genetic studies of deaths from all causes able to show the shape of the curve at low intake; or a long-term randomized trial of drinking a little against not drinking. None of the sources read reports these.
